Equivalently, with \(t\) hours after 8:00:

**SQLite** is the right default for a self-hosted single-user web app.

It is one file, zero extra processes, trivial backups (copy the file), and fast enough for one person. Use it when the app is local or lightly used, writes are modest, and you want simple deploy and restore. WAL mode handles concurrent reads fine; a single user rarely hits write-lock pain.

**PostgreSQL** is the right call when you need real concurrency (background jobs plus the UI writing at once), richer types and constraints, full-text search, JSON operators you will actually use, row-level security, or a path to multi-user later without a migration. It costs a running service, auth, backups, and upgrades.

**Rule of thumb:** start with SQLite unless you already know you need Postgres features or concurrent writers. Switching later is a migration, not a rewrite, if you keep SQL portable and avoid SQLite-only quirks.

When you ask an AI a question, it does not start from a blank page. It first reads everything you sent—the question, any earlier messages, and instructions about how to behave—and turns that text into an internal form it can work with. That reading step takes time and computing power, especially when the same long instructions or documents are sent again and again.

Prompt caching is a shortcut for that repeated work. If the beginning of a new request matches something the system has already processed, it can reuse that earlier result instead of reading those words all over again. The AI still answers your new question normally; it just skips redoing the shared setup. That usually makes replies faster and cheaper, a bit like remembering a recipe you use every day instead of rereading the whole cookbook each time.

The loop never includes 10, and the divisor doesn’t match the count.

`range(1, 10)` yields `1` through `9` (the stop is exclusive), so `total` is `45`. Dividing by `10` treats that as ten values, so you get `4.5` instead of the mean of those nine numbers (`5.0`), or of `1` through `10` (`5.5`).

If you want the average of `1` through `10`:

```python
total = 0
for i in range(1, 11):
    total += i
print(total / 10)
```

If you meant the average of what the loop already sums (`1`–`9`), keep the range and divide by `9` (or by the actual count).

A VPN and a reverse proxy solve different problems. Self-hosters often use both.

**VPN**  
A VPN builds an encrypted tunnel so a client joins a private network (or sends traffic through a remote gateway). After you connect, you can reach hosts and ports as if you were on that LAN—SSH, file shares, databases, admin UIs—not only websites. Typical self-host uses: remote access to a home or lab network without exposing every service to the internet, site-to-site links between locations, and protecting traffic on untrusted Wi-Fi. Common tools: WireGuard, Tailscale/Headscale, OpenVPN, IPsec.

**Reverse proxy**  
A reverse proxy sits in front of servers and accepts inbound connections (usually HTTP/HTTPS), then forwards them to backend apps. Clients talk to the proxy; they do not join your private network. Typical self-host uses: one public IP and ports 80/443 for many services (virtual hosts), TLS certificates, path- or hostname-based routing, basic auth or SSO in front of apps, and sometimes caching or rate limits. Common tools: Caddy, Nginx, Traefik, HAProxy.

**When to use which**

| Goal | Prefer |
| --- | --- |
| Reach private services from your own devices without opening them to the world | VPN |
| Publish a website or API to anyone on the internet | Reverse proxy |
| Several web apps, one domain or one set of ports, HTTPS | Reverse proxy |
| Non-HTTP protocols (SMB, arbitrary TCP, full LAN access) | VPN |
| Hide admin panels from the public internet | VPN (or proxy + strong auth, if they must be public) |

They compose well: put public sites behind a reverse proxy, and keep everything else on a VPN so only your devices can reach it. A reverse proxy is not a substitute for a VPN if you need arbitrary private-network access, and a VPN is a poor way to serve the public web.

QWERTY won by lock-in, not by being the fastest layout.

Christopher Latham Sholes and colleagues developed it in the 1870s for mechanical typewriters. The usual story—that it was meant to slow typists so the machine wouldn’t jam—is only partly right. Early typewriters used swinging typebars that could collide if nearby keys were hit in quick succession. QWERTY spread common letter pairs apart so those bars were less likely to clash. It was a reliability fix for a mechanical constraint, not a layout optimized for finger speed or home-row efficiency.

It became the standard because it got there first and stayed:

- **Remington adopted it.** The Remington No. 2 (late 1870s) used QWERTY and was the first widely sold typewriter. Training, manuals, and sales all followed that machine.
- **Typists learned one layout.** Once schools, businesses, and operators standardized on QWERTY, switching meant retraining everyone and replacing equipment.
- **Competitors copied it.** Other makers matched QWERTY so their machines could use the existing pool of trained typists.
- **Computers inherited it.** When keyboards moved to electric typewriters and then computers, the mechanical jam problem was gone, but the installed base of people and habits was not. Changing the default would have imposed a huge coordination cost for a modest speed gain.

Later layouts such as Dvorak were designed more deliberately for speed and reduced finger travel, and some studies found advantages for trained users. They never displaced QWERTY because the benefit wasn’t large enough, or certain enough, to overcome retraining costs and the fact that almost every keyboard, OS, and typing course already assumed QWERTY. That is classic path dependence: an early, “good enough” choice becomes sticky even after the original reason for it disappears.

The 1858 Transatlantic Telegraph Cable, led by Cyrus West Field and laid by HMS Agamemnon and USS Niagara meeting mid-ocean, was the first attempt to span the Atlantic and briefly carried ceremonial messages between Queen Victoria and President James Buchanan. It failed after only 732 messages in three weeks, but it proved the concept, and a permanent cable followed in 1866.
The 1858 cable transmitted 732 messages before failing. Cyrus West Field led the project.
